title: Classical Nahuatl — a demo language family

languages.name: Classical Nahuatl
languages.notes: The root of this demo family: Classical Nahuatl as recorded in 16th-century colonial sources for the Aztec capital and its hinterland. All 221 headwords are converted from the Wiktionary Classical Nahuatl lemmas; long vowels are marked with length, ⟨h⟩ is the glottal stop, and ⟨tz, ch, tl, ll, hu, qu⟩ map to their standard IPA values. There are no historical sound changes — synchronic allophony only.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

languages.name: Proto-Balto-Slavic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Speculative branch one: the Classical Nahuatl lexicon pushed through Proto-Balto-Slavic-style changes — Winter-type lengthening before the glottal stop, the RUKI sibilant rule, the first palatalization of velars before front vowels, and a long-vowel swap between ā and ō.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: The labio-velar loses its lip-rounding, as the pre-Balto-Slavic labialized velars merge with plain *k.
First palatalization applied as a sequential child, so the velar freshly derived from kʷ still palatalizes before front vowels (Proto-Slavic *kʷ > č).
First palatalization of native /k/ before front vowels (Proto-Slavic *k > č, *ḱ > č).

soundChanges.notation: s > ʃ / [l w j k i] _
soundChanges.note: RUKI law, retuned to the Nahuatl sonorants: /s/ becomes [ʃ] after *l, *w, *j, velars, and *i.
Winter's law retuned: a vowel lengthens before the phone that came from Nahuatl ⟨h⟩ (the glottal stop).
The glottal stop disappears once it has triggered lengthening, closing the Winter chain in one parallel pass.
Baltic colouring: *ā takes the ō slot of the proto-language.
…while older ō descends as *ā; the two long back vowels trade their tokens in the same parallel pass.

languages.name: Baltic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Balto-Slavic Nahuatl in the Baltic direction: geminate laterals degeminate, the palatoalveolar affricate stays, and /w/ hardens to [v] as in Latvian and Lithuanian intervocalic w.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: The dental affricate simplifies to a plain fricative, as Baltic does not keep *ts.
Baltic hardens /w/ to the obstruent [v].
Geminate laterals degeminate, as in the quotation of Baltic *lː > *l.

languages.name: Lithuanian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Lithuanian-style daughter: the surviving affricate becomes the sh-sibilant, s palatalizes before front vowels (Lithuanian s > š), and Baltic *ā backs to o.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Proto-Balto-Slavic *č yields Lithuanian š.
Lithuanian assibilates /s/ before front vowels, giving its characteristic še/ši.
Baltic *ā backs and rounds to Lithuanian o (Latvian keeps ā).

languages.name: Latvian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Latvian-style daughter: the affricate falls back to [s] (Latvian č > s) and n palatalizes to ň before front vowels, as in Latvian ņem and ziņa.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Proto-Balto-Slavic *č deaffricates in Latvian.
Latvian palatalizes /n/ to ņ before front vowels (ņem, ziņa).

languages.name: Slavic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Balto-Slavic Nahuatl in the Slavic direction: lateral affricates flatten into plain laterals, inherited geminate laterals degeminate, and the palatoalveolar affricate merges with the fricative series.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Proto-Slavic-style weakening of pre-Slavic *č.
Lateral affricates are not tolerated in Slavic onset/coda shape: *tl > l.
Proto-Slavic degeminates inherited *lː, leaving a single lateral.

languages.name: Polish Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Polish-style daughter: laterals — plain and geminate — vocalize to the famous Polish ł, w hardens to orthographic w = [v], and long *ō rises to u as in the history of Polish ó.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Proto-Slavic *l yields Polish ł [w], and geminate lː vocalizes with it.
Polish orthographic w is the voiced fricative [v].
Long *ō rises to u, the historical source of Polish ó = [u].

languages.name: Russian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Russian-style daughter: the East-Slavic loss of phonemic vowel length merges every long vowel into its short partner, *w hardens to [v], and prothesis gives word-initial o a consonantal onset (Russian восемь < *osmь).

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: East-Slavic prothetic [v/w] before *o (cf. Russian восьмой, восемь).
Russian loses the inherited long/short vowel opposition; *ā merges with a.
Long *ē shortens to e, the later fate of Proto-Slavic ě in Russian.
Long *ī shortens to i.
Long *ō shortens to o.
East Slavic hardens Proto-Slavic *w to the fricative [v].

languages.name: Czech Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Czech-style daughter: long *ē rises to í, long *ō backs and rises to ů [uː], and n palatalizes to ň before i/í, as in Czech ni and ní.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Proto-Slavic *ē gives Czech í.
Long *ō becomes Czech ů [uː], the historical source of the ringed u.
Czech palatalizes /n/ to ň before i/í (ni, ní).

languages.name: Proto-Arabic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Speculative branch two: the Classical Nahuatl lexicon reworked the way the Semitic family shaped Proto-Arabic — emphatic uvulars from labio-velars, voiced affrication of č, thāʾ from the dental affricate, and the Semitic p > f.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: The labio-velar back-shifts to the uvular /q/, the Arabic emphatic stop.
The voiceless affricate finds its voiced partner, Arabic jīm.
The dental affricate spirantizes to /θ/, Arabic thāʾ.
Semitic roots have no lateral affricate: *t͡ɬ debuccalizes into a plain sibilant.
Semitic *p > f (Hebrew/Arabic pā > fā).

languages.name: Peninsular Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Arabic Nahuatl with a Peninsular colouring: short e lowers to [ɛ] as in Central Arabian dialects, and the diphthongs *aw and *aj monophthongize to ō and ē.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Peninsular short-e lowering.
Peninsular *aw monophthongizes to ō, as in Najdi and Gulf Arabic.
Peninsular *aj monophthongizes to ē, as in Najdi and Gulf Arabic.

languages.name: Gulf Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Gulf-style daughter: uvular /q/ stops to [g], jīm deaffricates to [j], and kāf palatalizes to [t͡ʃ] before front vowels, all as in Gulf Arabic.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Gulf dialects front the uvular /q/ to [g] (qāl > gāl).
Gulf jīm is realized as the palatal glide [j] (mōj 'wave').
Gulf kāf palatalizes to [t͡ʃ] before front vowels (k > č).

languages.name: Bedouin Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Bedouin-style daughter: jīm stays as a palatal glide, uvular *q fronts to [g], and the glottal stop is lost, as in the Bedouin/Najdi dialects.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Bedouin jīm yields the palatal [j] rather than [d͡ʒ].
Najdi and Bedouin *q is realized as [g] (qāl > gāl).
Historical Najdi Arabic deletes the glottal stop outside learned borrowings.

languages.name: Levantine Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Arabic Nahuatl with the Levantine colouring: uvular /q/ merges with the glottal stop (qāl > ʔāl), jīm becomes [ʒ], and *aw/*aj monophthongize to ō/ē.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Levantine /q/ is realized [ʔ] in native words.
Levantine jīm is the voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ].
Levantine *aw monophthongizes to ō.
Levantine *aj monophthongizes to ē.

languages.name: Lebanese Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Lebanese-style daughter: thāʾ stops to [t] (Lebanese θ > t), short e lowers to [ɛ], and Levantine jīm is inherited as [ʒ].

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Lebanese /θ/ > [t] (thāʾ stopping).
Lebanese short-e lowering.

languages.name: Palestinian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Palestinian-style daughter: kāf affricates to [t͡ʃ] before front vowels — the signature Palestinian k-alternation — thāʾ spells plain [s], and Levantine jīm is inherited as [ʒ].

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Palestinian /θ/ > [s].
Palestinian kāf palatalizes before front vowels (θ/market k > t͡ʃ as in Palestinian kaškāš).

languages.name: Egyptian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Arabic Nahuatl with the Egyptian colouring: thāʾ blends into plain [s] (Egyptian-i-huu th > s), and *aw/*aj monophthongize to ō/ē as in Cairene Arabic.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Egyptian /θ/ is realized [s].
Egyptian *aw monophthongizes to ō.
Egyptian *aj monophthongizes to ē.

languages.name: Cairene Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Cairene-style daughter: jīm stops to [g] (Cairene gāla), uvular /q/ merges with ʔ, and long i rises the classic eː colouring (Cairene ī > eː).

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Cairene jīm is the plain stop [g].
Cairene colours long ī toward eː.
Cairene merges /q/ with the glottal stop.

languages.name: Saidi Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Saidi-style daughter: the uvular gives way to [g] (Upper-Egyptian qāl > gāl), and jīm is the palatal stop [ɟ] of southern Upper Egypt.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Saidi /q/ > [g].
Southern Upper Egyptian jīm is the voiced palatal stop [ɟ].

languages.name: Maghrebi Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Arabic Nahuatl with the Maghreb colouring: thāʾ stops to [t] (Maghrebi θ > t) and jīm dots to [ʒ] (French-influenced Maghreb ż).

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Maghrebi /θ/ > [t].
Maghrebi jīm is the French-debt [ʒ].

languages.name: Moroccan Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Moroccan-style daughter: long e loses its length to [e] and the post-alveolar sibilant folds into plain [s] the way Moroccan Arabic š > s in loans.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Moroccan Arabic shortens the e-vowel length.
Moroccan š folds into [s], as in Moroccan ši > si.

languages.name: South Arabian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-3 daughter of Proto-Arabic Nahuatl with the South-Arabian colouring: jīm deaffricates to [d] as in the Mahri/Hadhi dialects, and word-final hamza is lost.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: South Arabia's jīm falls back to a stop [d].
Word-final hamza is dropped in the South Arabian dialects.

languages.name: Mahri Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gen-4 Mahri-style daughter: the velar spirantizes to [x] (Mahri k > x), and Arabic *q yields the emphatic [kʼ], the Modern South Arabian reflex of ḳ.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Mahri spirantizes /k/ to the rich velar fricative [x].
Mehri ḳ is the velar ejective [kʼ], the regular reflex of Arabic *q.
